title: Saying amin
hookLine: aloud or silently after the Fatiha, by school

cards: The imam reaches the end of the Fatiha in a loud prayer. The last line rings out, and in some mosques the whole hall answers with one long word, rolling from the front rows to the back like a wave hitting a wall: aameen.
Visitors sometimes jump. In another mosque, same line, same voice, and then nothing you can hear. Lips move, maybe.
The hall is silent. Today, one word, and the ways it is said, or not said.

teach.b: The Fatiha closes, in Pickthall's words, "Not the (path) of those who earn Thine anger nor of those who go astray." Right after that line comes amin, a short request that Allah answer what was just asked.
It isn't a verse of the Qur'an; it's the response to one.

teach.h: WITH THE AMIN OF THE ANGELS.
teach.b: Why it matters: in a report in Sahih al-Bukhari, the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ says that when the imam says amin, the people should say it too, because whoever's amin falls together with the amin of the angels has past sins forgiven.
A small word, with a large promise around it. Then the question the report doesn't settle: how loud?
Shafi'i and Hanbali scholars teach that in the loud prayers, the imam and those behind him say it aloud. That's the wave. They point to reports of the Prophet raising his voice with it.

Hanafi scholars teach saying it quietly, as a supplication, and supplication, they say, is best kept low. Maliki teaching also keeps it quiet, with its own discussion of whether the imam says it in the loud prayers.
Last, the Ja'fari school. Its jurists hold that amin is not part of the prayer, so it isn't said there at all; Shia worshippers pass straight from the Fatiha to the next surah.
So one hall answers with a wave, another under the breath, and a third moves straight on.

how: After the Fatiha, Shafi'i and Hanbali congregations say amin aloud in the loud prayers; Hanafis and Malikis say it quietly; in the Ja'fari school it is not said in the prayer.

o: the response after the Fatiha, said aloud, quietly, or not at all
a call the imam gives to straighten the rows
the closing verse of the Fatiha, recited by the imam

s: amin is the last verse of the Fatiha
it isn't a verse of the Qur'an; it's the response that comes right after the Fatiha.
a report in Sahih al-Bukhari links the people's amin with the amin of the angels
whoever's amin falls together with the angels' has past sins forgiven, the report says.
a silent hall after the Fatiha means the people forgot
Hanafis and Malikis say it quietly, and the Ja'fari school doesn't say it at all.

games.q: you're visiting a Hanafi mosque, used to a hall that roars amin. the Fatiha ends and the room is silent. what do you do?
o: say it as you were taught, without making a scene.
games.why: both ways are careful readings of the same reports. the Hanafi hall says it quietly; a visitor's amin is a difference, not an error.

practice: Sit quietly and think of one thing you hope for today, something small and real, and hold it. Notice the difference between saying a hope out loud and keeping it under your breath.
If you pray, you can say amin in the way your school teaches.

wordCard.voice: Saying amin. The response after the Fatiha: aloud in loud prayers for Shafi'is and Hanbalis, quietly for Hanafis and Malikis, not said in the Ja'fari school. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: amin, said after the Fatiha, asking Allah to answer.

carryVoice: Your line: aloud or silent. The same word can be a wave or a whisper. Until tomorrow.
